projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Alvin H. Karges was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Alvin H. Karges. Mr. Karges served in the U.S. Army with the 101st Airborne Division, 327th Regimental Headquarters Company. He served in the European theater and his highest rank was T-4. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Karges' home in Cleveland Heights, Ohio on August 4th, 2002. Al was 90 at the time of this recording. Where were you living when America entered the war?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Where was I living?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I was living -- when I was drafted I lived on 99th Street in Cleveland, Ohio. And what I wanted to tell you was at that time I was drafted from there, I was dating Margery, and I am not on the Cleveland list of those who went and I'm not on the Cleveland Heights list. So actually it's kind of a between, living in Cleveland and Cleveland Heights because, as I think I said before, we were married when I was in service. And when I came back on a furlough, even before we were married, we were engaged, and I came back on a furlough, that's when I had the orders to report from my dad -- he got a telephone call or what -- to report immediately to Fort Bragg. I had been at Cleburne. And I went to Fort Bragg to radio school. And I was at radio school -- when I came home, we got married anyway. And how her mother arranged it all, I don't know, but she surely did. We had a nice wedding at Wade Park Manor. And we left on a honeymoon to go to Fort Benning. I'd never been there before, as I think I told you before. We got down to Fort Benning late at night and we looked for a telephone -- a hotel with a match in the telephone book. It was dark kind of. So we finally got to the hotel. And, of course, we couldn't afford to stay there any length of time. So after I got situated in camp, Margie went out and looked around and put her name in places for a place to live. And we found -- she found a place. Two older ladies had a large home in Columbus, Georgia, which is right near Fort Benning. And I would -- they had like a flatbed truck would go around like a bus and pick up a lot of the soldiers that were training at Fort Bragg and take us to camp and then bring us home at night, see. So we were there three months. And, while I was there, I was asked to be interviewed for officers training school. And there were three of us that were from the 101st that were at this radio school. And I was fortunate enough to be selected to go to officers training school. However, our outfit was really hot to go overseas and my company commander would not release me to go to OCS. So Margie was pregnant and so she came home, oh, about a month or so before I left Bragg to go to Camp -- oh, up in New York.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Shanks?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Not Shanks?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, I think it was Shanks. And, from there, we got ready to go overseas. And I remember they said if you need -- this is kind of a cute story -- if you need any equipment, go over to the supply room and they'll give you what you need. So one of the fellows says, "Yeah, I'm going to get a new pair of jump boots." So he went over there and the fellow said, the supply sergeant says, "Fellow, where you're going you won't need jump boots." So, anyway, that's just kind of a little side story.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before we get too far, when did you go into the 101st?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Well, see, I was in the 82nd when I was at Cleburne.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you drafted originally?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Oh, yes, I was originally drafted.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This would be what? Do you remember exactly about when that was or close to when it was?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: When I was drafted?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: The month you mean?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, okay, the year, roughly. '42?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I suppose, yeah; yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: A few months after Pearl Harbor or something like that?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I guess, yeah. My mind is a little bit --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: So, anyway, as I tell you, this is kind of piecemeal so it doesn't really fit together.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's okay. You started out in the 82nd and then you were transferred to the 101st?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: That's right. Lee, I think, was the commander of the first airborne who started it with the 82nd. I remember when we were all in a group in the 82nd we said, "Now you're airborne. You don't have to march anymore." "Oh, yeah," we thought, "that's great." So anyway, as I said, my basic training was at Cleburne. And then, when I came home on a furlough from Cleburne, my outfit -- no. Or was I at Bragg? I don't remember whether I was at Cleburne or Bragg when I came home to get -- supposedly to get married. We were told we'd have a week or two when it was only a couple days like. But anyway, to get back to Camp Shanks, I -- we weren't up there too long. And I remember them putting us in a -- getting in a train with all the shades down. And they took us down -- see, I was born and raised in New Jersey, actually, so I was familiar with New York because I'd worked there. They took us down to some port where they put us on a boat and took us across to New York to get ready to go into the transport to go overseas. And that was the most miserable trip I ever took. And I don't even -- my son loves sailing, belongs to the yacht club and all, and I don't even want to go near a boat. We were in the bottom of this boat, way down below. They had drills, you know, in case something happened. You were supposed to be able to get up to the deck but you could never get up there. You could never get off that boat because there was so many guys on that boat. And, as I told you, it took us ten days, and it explains in here, about ten days to go over to England. And on the way over, our convoy was attacked, but I never heard of any of the ships being attacked. However, the steering on the boat that the 401st was on almost ran into us. They had a steering problem and they had to turn around and go back to Newfoundland. So the group that we were on took ten days to go. So they joined us later on over in England. So now --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And that's England. And, according to that, in September of '43?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yeah; uh-huh. And then I remember getting off the boat in England, thank goodness. And they got us in a group and we marched down this road a little ways and then up a hill to Camp Renneker, which was an Army camp at the top of this hill, which is now, I understand, a supermarket out there somewhere. And then we did a lot of training there. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were the people like in England?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Very nice. Very, very nice people. I spent some time with a couple that lived down the street, an older couple, somehow. They lived a little ways down the street from the camp. You could walk down there. And I think we were down there for dinner one time. And as far as the people are concerned, great; great. I didn't -- I don't remember how long I was at Camp Renneker, but I went in -- I know I visited London once. I was not a traveler. I kind of stayed kind of home. And I remember also, when we got to Renneker, they had these barracks. And there was just wooden two-by-four beds, you know, and straw mattresses. I had to get used to that. And I had the upper bunk and the fellow below me, I think, was a fellow by the name of Rickenthal (ph), a little Jewish fellow from New York. And we'd go up to the pub up the street. And I remember the pub. And they have the family room, you know, at one end of the pub where the husbands and wives would go, and then they have the other at the bar. And I didn't care for -- I don't care for beer, period. And I didn't like English ale much, so I didn't drink too much of that. Gin and tonic was -- gin is what I drink now. But, I mean, I drank a little gin and orange then. And then I remember going to this marshalling area to make the attack, for D-Day. And I remember we were all intense. And the officers' tent was right the same as our tent. And I remember Major -- not Major -- General Taylor was our General at that time. And I remember him jumping over the tent ropes, running around, so forth and so on. A very active man. And I remember D-Day, before D-Day, they got us into a huge field, the 101st. And at that time Eisenhower walked between the rows. And I was as close to you as to Eisenhower. And he spoke to the fellow in front of me and he said, "Where are you from, fellow?" And a very fine gentleman. I have the greatest admiration for General Eisenhower. He was just a regular guy. And I remember then that we -- as I said, I didn't go into Normandy. I went by boat, by an LST, landing craft -- landing ship infantry -- LSI, I guess it is. And I remember getting on the boat. But we'd been on a boat like that before in some training exercises that we had. But we never did actually get down off the larger ship until D-Day. As I told you, that's the first time I ever dropped those rope ladders down. And I went down the rope ladder and got into an LCI, landing craft infantry. That's a smaller boat, kind of like a scow, and the ends drop down. And I had a radio on my back, a large radio, and I had my M-1. And, of course, you're loaded with ammunition and you weigh a ton. And the old boat -- I remember the old little boat going, like this, while you're trying to get down. And we got into the boats and we hit the -- there was a lot of -- oh, the battleships were lined up along the shore there and firing like crazy. I mean, you could see the fire -- oh, I said it looked like it was from here to that house -- shooting out of the end of these great big guns. And you didn't think of it at that time, but I wonder now how the hell anybody could live on what they threw in there. In fact, some of the shells -- well, I guess, when they landed, make a hole about half as big as the basement of this house. They were big shells they were throwing in. So, anyway, we climbed down there. And, as I said, when we got in this LCI, we went as far as we could. We hit a sandbar or whatever. And the guy said, "End of the line, guys," and you jumped off. So I said I didn't swim. And there was water up to here. And I put my radio and my gun over my head and waded in. And, as I think I told you, there was a young guy next to me -- there was a lot of people moved and so forth, floating around, dead and whatnot -- and he kept -- he said to me, "Why don't they pick these guys up?" And I told him, "Never mind. Get your ass on the beach. Don't worry about those guys. Somebody will take care of them." After that -- I don't know who the guy was, or even before, because there's a lot of confusion going on. So we got on the beach and we got up to this road. We gathered on the beach and we go up this road and we turned to the right and we went up about a half a mile and they said, "Whoa. Hey, you've gone the wrong way." But this was a group. This must have been 50, 60 guys. So we turned around. We went the other way and finally got our location on the beach. And, I mean, the beach was sand where we spent that night. In fact, in the morning, the next morning, it didn't bother you. You're soaking wet, but, I mean, you don't even think about it. To me, I didn't. It wasn't in my mind that I was wet. You were just thinking about you had a job to do and you were going to do it. So, anyway, the next morning I got up. We woke up and got out of our foxholes. Of course, the beaches were where a lot of the wounded were and so forth. And a German plane came over and was going to strafe the beaches, a small plane. And it was shot at, hit. And this guy's coming down. He's on fire. And, of course, some guy next to me is running out with his rifle. And there's a hell of a lot of our guys going after him. I says, "Put your goddamn rifle up." And I knocked it out of his hands. He could hit one of our guys. "Don't worry. We'll get the guy." Whatever happened to him, I don't know. But it was, I'd say, oh, from here maybe to the corner or a little further away where he came down in his parachute. But he was on fire. I don't think he lived. And then the next couple of days -- I don't remember the time again. It slips my mind. But I was selected to go on a patrol to make contact with the Second Battalion. See, you were on the beaches and you had to get organized. And we went on -- we started out. There was myself and my radio operator, this little guy Rickenthal (ph), and myself. And we had some recon men. I don't know how many. Of course, see, I was in Regimental Headquarters and the recon unit and the radio unit, you know, they are all together, and the medical unit, in Regimental Headquarters. And we started out through this woods. And then there was an open field. And we was about to go across and some G.I. comes and says, "You can't go there. There's Germans on the other side. You have to go around. You can't go through an open field," which we should have known anyway. But I wasn't leading the patrol; the Colonel was. So we did. We got around the patrol -- or the woods there. And, of course, it's just kind of dirt roads over there. And where two roads came together, there had been a skirmish. There was a lot of blood there and a couple of guys had to remove it. But they say you have to just keep going. They weren't alive anyway. So we kept going. And I'd say we left in the morning around 8 o'clock, I guess. And I would say we made our contact with the Second Battalion, oh, I would say, about 1 o'clock. It took us that long. We were going through woods and paths and stuff. Now, I say, on the patrol, there must have been 12, 15, maybe 20 guys. I don't exactly remember. We had some riflemen. And, as I said, I was a communication man. And they had wiremen, too, you know. And we made our contact. And then they put us in a truck. And I think it took us about 20 minutes to get back from where we started from. That's how long it took us to work our way. But, in a truck, you get somewhere in practically no time at all. And we stayed there -- again, I don't remember how long. But our first mission was Saint Mary Gleese, which is practically a church and a house, or whatever. That was the Division's --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Objective maybe?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: -- project to get there. So I remember going through Saint Mary Gleese. And we had some troubles. I'm talking about the regiment now. We came to a river. I think it was the Duve River. It wasn't a great wide river; not too big. And we were held up. And, as I -- this is rumor now. I didn't see it. I just saw the results of it. The head of our regiment was Colonel Ware. Colonel Ware was an older -- kind of an older man and not that active. I mean, like a father. And I understand we were held up there. And the reason is he got orders to cross the Duve River and he couldn't get them over and he was relieved of his command. That's when -- that's the story, I guess, because I never saw Colonel Ware after that. And at that time Colonel Harper from the 401st took over the 327th. He became the commander. And, from then on, he was our commander. In fact, he was the one who talked to the Germans when they said nuts and so forth.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: McCauliff (ph)?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: McCauliff (ph). He was the -- well, Taylor was really the General. But Taylor at that time was in this country for a holiday or something and McCauliff was running the outfit then. And, as I said -- see, our airborne unit is made up of three battalions and a Regimental Headquarters. And you had a radio sergeant in each one of the battalions and a radio operator. And we had two or three radio sergeants in Regimental Headquarters. That's where I was. And we didn't do too much. We did more -- actually, in combat, we did more listening than we did transmitting. Of course, backing off again, when I went to radio school, basically what you were doing was learning Morse Code, which we never used. It was always voice. But it was there, because you can destroy voice but you can't destroy Morse Code. I mean, it gets through almost anywhere. So it was always a backup for our communications to get through. And at that time I remember we were in the hedgerow country. And the hedgerow country is like that wall there, only instead of being nothing on top, there's bushes and stuff on top. And we would dig in our foxholes back at that wall. And then you'd listen at night and during the day you'd say -- you'd hear the shells coming over and exploding and you'd say, "Is it incoming mail or is it outgoing?" You know, keeping track. And I remember at the end of the -- kind of the end of that wall the Jeep was there and that's where you cooked a meal or anything on those stoves, the little stoves you had or whatever. It's not gasoline, but some kind of --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sterno?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Sterno, yeah. And we lived on K rations basically. We had some C rations, but mostly K. And, as I say, then we moved from there. The next move I remember, I was stationed in a little town -- oh, our mission there was to take the Presquile Le Caritan. That was our mission after we took Saint Mary Gleese. Our next mission was to take Caritan, which was a peninsula. And so halfway between the beaches and Caritan, I had a radio station, so-called. I mean, I had a radio set there. And it was a store. And it was in a little town; oh, again, three or four buildings. You crossed the street and there was a group of buildings. And the building we were in was empty. And we were on the upper floor. I don't know what was ever on the lower floor, but we were upstairs. And it had kind of a balcony overhanging the sidewalk. And I remember, when we first got there, I'd never seen so much armor go through 24 hours a day. Tanks and stuff just kept going through that road to get up to Caritan. That's what it was. And right across the street this woman owned a tavern, I guess you'd call it, or a restaurant, or whatever. And these little girls used to come over. And we had chocolate. And we'd drop them chocolate bars once in a while, just to, you know, be friendly with the kids and whatnot. I never met the woman. I probably saw her walking around. And so one night there must have been four or five of us working this radio station. We had shifts, you know. Somebody had to be on there all the time. We always had to have a cranker and a guy sending, see. So you actually took two guys to run the operation. So, anyway, to get back to this woman, it was dairy country and there was a lot of beef and stuff. She sent over steaks for all of us one night, which I thought was pretty damn nice. But, other than that, we lived on K rations. And one time we got some beans, dried beans, and we made them, and we shouldn't have ate them. I don't know if we didn't make them right or what. You ate those things and you thought you were going to explode. So we were there, I guess, a week and a half; maybe two weeks, three. I begin to lose perception of it. And then, from there, I think we went back to England. They had freed up Caritan and we went back to England to reorganize and so forth and get ready for the Holland invasion. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Before we get to that, did you land on Omaha Beach?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Utah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You landed on Utah. Okay.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Utah, right; yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And were you -- how early was it in that invasion?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Pardon me?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How early was it? First wave, second wave?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Oh, I would say we got there early evening.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Maybe from five to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: On the 6th? Is that right?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yeah; right. Oh, I remember, too, we were on this landing craft, the first, the big one, and I remember them coming over and telling us, "This is it. Don't take clothes off. Keep putting clothes on," they kept telling us. So, I mean, certain things stick in your mind, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And why were they saying that?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was it because of the gas-impregnated clothing?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I suppose, maybe. Or just to keep you -- well, you were going to jump into the water, and they probably knew it, to keep yourself. But to go back further, I think the worst trip was when I went over. I got up on the deck one time and I never saw -- this is on the transport taking us over. I never seen so many sick guys. I mean, you couldn't go in the john. The floor was just -- and the meals on that. It was an English ship and they give you sausage, but half of it was cereal in between. And it was just a miserable trip. Miserable.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you're back in England preparing for Market Square?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: That's right. Yes, yes, yes. And we went out to the airfield. I remember that. The guard -- there were planes there and the guards were in the back. And I have some pictures somewhere of us before. I think that's when we had a picture taken with some of us in the glider, standing there, getting ready to go over. And I remember that's the only time I flew into combat. I flew the English Channel and I remember -- beautiful. I mean, when you fly in a glider -- I don't know if you've ever flown in a glider, but it's -- oh, it almost peaceful. Take an airplane and it's vibrating. A glider, you know, you don't have all that noise and it's really -- it floats. It floats. So, anyway, going across the Channel wasn't bad. I saw one or two gliders that didn't make it. I mean, they went down for some reason. Either the tow rope broke or whatever it was. And we hit the field that we were supposed to land in. We must have been going a hundred miles an hour. You're not supposed to land a glider anywhere near that speed. In fact, I don't know if you're familiar with a glider, but the floor of a glider is like -- it looks like piano -- you know what piano wood looks like? Of course, it's very light. And we landed in a beet field and the beets just came right up. In fact, they don't -- you'd think they'd have a glider pilot and a second pilot. But they don't. And the officer sat. And that officer that sat in the front, I remember him. He was covered with beets and crap, right up through the floor, you know. No one was hurt in the landing. From our glider, I'm talking about. But every glider, you know, it has skids. It's supposed to crash land. But, you know, if there's a tree or something there, you either -- you just make the best of it. But I don't remember too many casualties. Well, you don't have time to look around. You've got a mission. After we landed, we gathered up the group together and hit the road. And we were walking up the road and the Dutch people were lined up on both sides of the road and they were giving us food and everything. And they gave me a white carrot. I never ate a raw white carrot. I did then. As we marched up the road, they were so happy to see us. And that was a pretty rough campaign for us. We -- we got caught once in, I think it was, near Eindhoven or -- I can't even remember the name of the town. But we pulled into this field. Again, the middle of the field was open. We were around the outside. But the Germans, apparently, were in some kind of a building in the town. And they spotted us and we got caught in an artillery barrage. I don't know if it was mortars or what it was. But we lost a lot of men and wounded. Fortunately, I was like from here to the driveway there. And it was bushes there. And then there was kind of a fence that had a wire, barbwire fence. But it was broken down, part of it. So I made for that. And, when I went under the fence, I caught my pack, but I got out. And I got into a ditch and laid down in the ditch until the barrage was over. And I remember hearing shrapnel pooping in the water around me. But fortunately none of it hit me. So -- and I'm trying to figure out where now. Oh, I think after we got -- what our exact mission was then, I'm not sure. But then we got back to Mourmelon. That was our camp in France. Our base camp was Mourmelon. But on one of them missions we were on -- I don't know if it was this one or another one -- we were in like a girls' school. It was a large home like. And one end was like these old glass windows. And it was kind of up on a hill. And it's kind of woodsy over there. And at night you could kind of hear this German tank squeaking around down below in the hills, see. So we were set up in this house. It was headquarters, Headquarters Company right there. And so one night we hear these screaming meemies. We hear this like siren. All of a sudden they hit that building, the glass. And we ducked out of the building and went in the front of the building. It was a stone building, so it was a good, solid building. And, in the basement, a lot of the people that lived there went in the basement before, you know, for protection. And actually that night a shell made a hole in the floor about that big and fell down into the basement and never exploded. Otherwise, we'd have been out. Because we saw it the next day when some British guys came that defused the bombs and that, to take that bomb out. That's when we saw the bomb. But I don't know whether -- I don't remember whether that was on that mission or whether it was another mission that we were on. But --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories about your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: My first baptism of fire was when I jumped in the water on an LS -- that landing craft. And there was shells coming over and there was a spattering of fire around. I don't want to sound like I'm brave, but everybody had a mission to do. They trained us. I mean, I laid down on a beach and I was soaking wet. If I get wet now and I get in a breeze, I've got a cold. That night I laid down in it and it didn't bother me. Things didn't seem to bother me that much. We were going up -- a couple things I remember, we were going up kind of a hill, advancing, and there was an American guy there. His whole chest was all blown out. He was laying there. I mean, you have a mission. The medics, today, they are supposed to do their job. You have your job to do. And one thing, the guys, they did their job. And I never -- I was thinking today, I never heard anybody complain. I really didn't. And some of the meals -- you ate what you had. Sometimes it was just a piece of cheese for lunch and crackers. But I never heard anybody bitching. I mean, they just seemed to -- I think, when I was ready to go overseas, I was in the best physical condition ever in my life. And I'd say a lot of that training helped me to live as long as I have, because I was always kind of athletic anyway. I mean, I was always active. I wanted to play basketball, football and tennis. I lived on a tennis court when I was a kid. And so I always kept myself pretty active. Which, I guess, again, I was fortunate. But another time, things that I remember, I remember seeing -- I don't remember where this was either. There was a German soldier laying on the ground. And he had his hands up and he was saying, "Vassa (ph), vassa (ph)." He'd been wounded and he wanted water. And things like that I remember. But -- and, as I told you, I remember that when we went into Bastogne -- oh, we were back from that campaign we were just talking about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Market Square?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Back in Mourmelon. And we were just, you know, R and R, getting equipment you needed and so forth and so on. And one afternoon about 4 o'clock, they said, or earlier in the afternoon, "At 4 o'clock you're going to get on trucks. We're going out of here." That was when we went up to Bastogne. And some of the guys didn't have the stuff they needed. I pulled a rifle belt. I mean, you just got in those trucks and away you went. And I remember the ride up there. I didn't see any enemy, but I understand certain parts of -- it was a huge convoy, and I guess certain parts of it had some trouble. But most of us got in. And, of course, as I say, I was in regiment again. And the battalions -- see, in an airborne unit, it's like this circle. You have no flanks. See, one of the basic things, when you're learning about infantry, is try to flank your enemy. So you take a lot of it so he's got to watch you over here instead of here. With an airborne unit, you never flanked because you're round. So Headquarters Unit was in the middle of that. So actually, when I was in Bastogne, I was kind of in the center of all this stuff. And what we were in -- you know these places where they rent out sections for storage? It's a long, low building. There was a row of buildings. They were well built, concrete. They build everything well over there. In fact, there was tile floors in this. And the sections might have been about as wide as -- a little wider than this, twice as wide as this porch. And so that's where we stayed, in there. And then we'd have to go out. It was wintertime. And, of course, the air was -- they couldn't get us supplies in because Air Corps couldn't see where they were dropping. So they finally did break through, in a couple days, I guess, and we dashed out to drop what they had gotten down and put it away. But we would have to go -- at that time we would have to go up and kind of help the battalion. Every couple of hours you'd go up and help somebody. And some of those guys -- see, we were in this building and we had some heat in there, a fire or something. I don't remember. They'd come in there and they had ice inside their shoes. I felt sorry for some of those guys. It was really rough up there. So finally we broke that. Well, as I said, while I was up there, I was sent out with a radio operator to an OP, which is beyond the front lines. That's an observation post. And we took turns. And I was up there a couple of days. And that's when I told you that Colonel was packed full of champagne. And with this big radio operator, we could hear what Patton was doing, coming to get us out. And, as I said, when we went into Bastogne, there were guys coming back. You know, they had broken through the front lines. And --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell me again. That Colonel found this champagne in Bastogne. Is that right?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: No. He brought some. How he got it in his Jeep, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: He brought it with him?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: He had 10 or 12 cases there in the basement. You know, at that time I didn't even think much about it because I'm a gin drinker. I'm not a champagne drinker and stuff. It didn't bother me that much. Your mind is different. But that night we were in this basement and we could look out and see the German patrols in their white suits. They knew we were there and we knew where they were. But we were never supposed to tell where we were, as far as the communications, never. But they never bothered us and we never bothered them. So they finally broke through us. I mean, we got out and we went to a little town called Emerald outside of Bastogne. And that's where I saw when Patton -- when I told you I saw Patton come in in his Jeep.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Tell that again. I don't know if we recorded that.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Well, I was there. We were kind of getting lost equipment again, kind of had an R and R on the way, towards Alsace. We were going down to Alsace from there. And Patton drove up in his Jeep, and his revolvers and whatnot, and he was talking to a few of the officers there. Of course, you don't go over and talk to anybody unless -- you know how the Army is. And, I'll tell you, my feeling today is every student should have one year military training before they ever go to college. It's discipline. And, boy, that means everything. I never heard anybody -- you get an order and you say, "Yes, sir," and you do it. And I'm a -- that's strong in my mind. In fact, both of my sons both graduated from college and I had them both go through ROTC. One of them actually saw some combat in Korea. And, in fact, he and his wife are coming over later on for a drink. And my other son was in the Medical Corps and he was stationed down in Texas. But he now lives in Maine. So all kind of -- and my oldest son is a real military buff. He goes back to the Civil War and can tell you everything, that the general had this and the Union Army did that. He's kind of a military strategist kind of guy. He loves it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you like Patton?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I mean, as far as I saw. I only saw him like I saw Eisenhower. I was fortunate enough to be close enough to these people to see actually that they were living persons and kind of how they acted and such. But I'm very strong -- because, you know, everybody says, "Oh, go in the Army and you're going to shoot somebody." There's so many jobs in the Army. I think there's 12 guys -- behind every guy that goes to the front, there's 12 guys behind him, supplying him. So there's so many jobs. And the same way with the women. There's a lot of jobs that men do in the Army that the women could do. So I think it wouldn't hurt to have military -- for everyone that gets out of our schools, one year of military service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you were surrounded in Bastogne, did it look pretty bleak? Did you think you would be overrun?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Oh, it was terrible. It was terrible. In fact, we were dive-bombed in this row of buildings. A German plane -- they didn't have that much left over. But a plane did come over and got the bomb on one section where the recon was. But nobody was in the building. But that kind of scared you, you know. Here you're surrounded and you could hear a lot of noise on the -- they had a -- this Colonel was in the armored unit and he had a -- his radio operator had a big set, much bigger than the one we had. And you could get a lot of -- hear a lot of the shooting and all this stuff coming through; you know, shelling. Not near us, not too near us, but around us. So -- but in Bastogne -- when we were in Bastogne, as I said, Red Vanteel (ph), who was Colonel Harper's personal radio operator, was a good friend of mine. And he was with Colonel Harper when they went down and talked to this -- giving surrender, you know, and he said nuts. So --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you guys know that that was the response? Did you know?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Did we know what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did they spread the word around the troops that they had responded; that there was a possibility of surrender and that that was the response?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I don't really remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You just knew you weren't surrendering.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: No; no. One thing I do remember, we must have been there at least a week because I remember a chaplain. Our chaplain was Gordon Cosby from one of the Carolinas. And I remember going to Christmas service there. He had a service in our little section and three or four -- oh, it must have been a dozen, maybe 20 guys went to the service in Bastogne. But I remember it was so damn cold in Bastogne. At the end of this row of buildings, there was kind of a lavatory where they had toilets. The toilets were busted right open from the cold. They just split them out. I mean, it was bitter cold out. Of course, we had tile floors. But we dug some of the tile out and made holes; you know, kind of foxholes. Well, not foxholes. Well, I guess you could call it a foxhole. Because, you know, Patton never believed in foxholes. He said that was the worst thing the Army ever did. He wanted to keep going, which maybe he had the right idea. But, as I say, I remember going up one road where they had a tank battle. And, boy, there were German tanks turned over and upside down and a couple other things. Things that you see, I don't remember where or what, but I remember seeing these things as you went, traveled from one place to another. And, oh, another thing, when we got into Normandy, and after we got settled a little bit and we were moving up, we went up to some kind of a field. And, again, it was a ditch and a big wall. And there was a big hole in the wall. I mean, oh, you could have driven a truck through it. So Red Vanteel (ph) and I were looking for a place to set up our radio. And this is in an apple orchard. And, boy, the ground is like concrete. It's hard as a rock. So first we looked in that ditch along there, see, right in front of this wall. Well, we thought, that may not be such a good place. So we were out in this apple orchard. We're starting to dig foxholes. All of a sudden we heard zing, zing. That's the first time in my life I have ever been directly shot at. It must have been some Germans on the other side of that wall. And they saw us in this open field or in an open area and they started shooting at us. But there were some other G.I.'s around there and they got -- when they heard it and saw it, they came. Everybody worked together. I mean, everybody was trying to protect everybody else. But that was the only time I was directly, actually. But, again, you know, as I said, if it happened now, you'd worry about sleeping at night. But I guess your mind is trained as well as your body. As I said, the training they gave us in Fort Bragg and Cleburne was tough. But it was good. I remember forced marches at night. I remember walking in my sleep. You know, they give you this training where you have to walk, you know, so long. You'd actually follow the guy in front of you. But if you come to a fork in the road and he goes the wrong way, you follow him. But it's excellent training; excellent training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the day the weather broke and you got your air support?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yes, because I remember them dropping those big -- I guess they call them bales or whatever. I don't even remember what was in them, because they had trucks there right away. As soon as they came down, why, you got into them. But, see, we weren't exactly in the center of Bastogne. This must have been a little bit on the outside, because I guess they did a lot of bombing in the center. You know, a lot of the buildings were torn down and whatever. But I saw enough of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So what was next after that, then?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: After Bastogne, we came back to -- oh, no, after -- what happened in Bastogne, you know, after we got free, we attacked. We attacked with what we had. We attacked. So the Germans didn't expect that. They thought, you know, that's it. As I say, after they started to attack, we went back. And then the 401st, I think, came in and they pushed ahead with us. And we were somehow -- I don't remember if it was after Bastogne, directly after Bastogne, or when we got a little relief from Bastogne that we went down to Alsace. And we were down there in a house. And I remember two or three of us were in this house. We were stationed in that area. And they had a mess hall, kind of a mess hall down there. It wasn't near the combat zone. And so this woman, a very nice woman, she said, oh, how bad the German soldiers were. They were washing their feet in her kitchen sink and all this stuff. And she said, "If you boys" -- they were cooking chickens up in there. She said, "If one of you fellows will go up and just bring me back the chicken feet," she says, "I'll make you the best chicken soup you ever had." Some guy went up and got them and, boy, it was great. But, I mean, some people, all over the world, everybody isn't -- the civilian population isn't at war so much. I think people like to help other people. And then, after we got back -- I don't remember when we were in Alsace. We went back to Mourmelon anyway. And when I was back at Mourmelon, I was in charge of communications there. Like I had a wireman and a couple of radiomen. They didn't need the radiomen, really, because we were just watching. Equipment was ready to be put into trucks to be moved up. And so these new replacement officers would come into camp and they'd have to ask me, "Can you get me a phone?" and stuff like that. So we were there, oh, a couple of weeks, I guess. And then we went up to -- we piled on and got orders to move our equipment and go up to Bastogne. Not Bastogne. Where Hitler's hideout was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The Eagles Nest? Berchtesgaden?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yeah, Berchtesgaden, that's right. After that, it was moving pretty fast then. I remember another part when we were somewhere, we went across the Nijmegen Bridge to a YMCA and we were able to get showers. We never had a chance to get many showers. You just had the clothes you had on and lived in them. So I remember going across that Nijmegen Bridge. And there were big holes and you had to be careful the trucks didn't fall down. They blew it up, you know. And, as I say, I can't tell exactly what sequence these things happened in, but I remember certain things that happened. Anyway, when we got to -- oh, when we went up to Berchtesgaden, it took us about two days to get up there. And I remember I was laying on the top of a canvas on a truck. That's the way I rode up there, with the equipment down below. There were two or three trucks. And we'd pull into these little towns at night, one night on the way up, and just rested there before we went on to the next day. When we got up to Berchtesgaden, we lived in hotel rooms and they had women that made our bed. I was in a nice little hotel. And I was on the second floor and I had a little porch up there. And they treated us royally when we got up there. And I got a chance to go up to the Eagles Nest. But it was, by the time I got there -- halfway up they had a great big bronze door where the elevator would take you up, you know. But the elevator wasn't even working, so we had to climb up. That's the first time I ever remember sweating on the ground and climbing up a mountain to get into the snow. But it sat practically -- you know, this was his house and you couldn't get there but certain little ways because it was secluded right on the top of a mountain. But halfway up he had a home. But they had blown the hell out of that, too. But when I got there, a few pieces of furniture were there. That's about all. Most of the G.I.'s that got there first, you know, they took out what they wanted, I suppose. The only thing I brought back was a German flag, which my oldest son wanted. I gave it to him. And he had some furniture in storage somewhere and they had a fire and it burnt up. It was the only thing I brought back. But it was quite an experience. And, as I say, for me it was a real education. You leave home and live with completely strange people all the way. You had to make friends. I made some very good friends. Don Hastings from out Estabule (ph) way. He started out with me at Cleburne and he went into the Rangers and was wounded. And we got together after the war, a couple of us. Another fellow, Carl Shaffer (ph), was in the anti-tank unit, which was part of Regimental Headquarters. He lived in Oleria (ph). They both died. But we used to get together on the holidays and have a little nuts-night dinner or whatever you want to call it. And Carl Shaffer married a very nice English girl. A very nice woman. And Don Hastings, I heard of his wife -- well, he died about ten years ago. But we used to visit him occasionally out in Paisley. It isn't Paisley. It's some little town and I can't think of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything with your buddies for entertainment to relieve the tension or anything when you were over there?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Not too much. Oh, what we did, we'd go out and try to find places to get some booze. But like one night we went out. It was Carl Shaffer and myself and two other guys. I don't remember who they were. And they had heard that this man in this little town worked at the officers' PX, an officers' club, and they had booze there and he could get us a bottle of booze. So, anyway, we started out this night. One of the guys knew where the house was. We walked up these roads and so forth and knocked on the door. He says, "Yes?" And we told him what we were looking for and he says, "Well, you know, I don't have any. But I do have some good booze, but it's not American booze." And he gave us a bottle of something that when you drank it your head got warm like that. We started down the road and we finished that bottle by the time we got to camp. And I'm telling you, we were really loaded. And the next day, you'd take a drink of water and you're loaded all over again. But, I mean, it was -- that's about what we did. We'd go out and drink somewhere. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any USO shows coming around you?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yeah, in England. In England. But overseas -- and as far as seeing Bob Hope or any of those shows -- I'll tell you, an airborne unit, especially the 101st, we were too busy. The only time we didn't have something to do was when we were R and R, getting ready for another mission. They kept us -- we didn't do a lot of training. After we got into combat, we didn't do any training. But, like they say, don't go into buildings, when they're teaching you, you know, so we didn't, because you wanted to get out of the rain or out of the snow or whatever. And one night I remember I slept in a pigsty. And that was one of the cleanest places I slept in in Holland. It was a cement -- a cement building about as big as this porch. And there were little like bathtubs, a whole row of them, and they were clean and white. I put my sleeping bag down there and I felt real safe. But, I mean, things like that stay in my mind more than -- some of the people, I guess, can go right through the routine of just what they did. But I don't. But, in talking to the fellow next door, he says, "Weren't you scared?" Well, I guess you're scared, but you had something in your mind; you've got to get there, you've got a job to do. And, sure, when the shells were coming in, you were fighting. But when they were over you thought, "Well, we didn't get hit." That's about the way you have to look at it, I guess. The same way with -- when I think of it now, I did the most stupid things ever being in the airborne, especially in the gliders. The paratroopers used to laugh at us and say we were nuts and we used to say they're nuts. Because, when you come down in a glider -- that's why they don't use them anymore, because they're dead. When they land, they crashed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have an option? Could you have been a paratrooper?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I think so. All I remember -- here's another thing I don't understand. They said you volunteer for airborne. All I remember is one time they said, "You're airborne." I don't remember saying, "Hey, I want to be airborne." All I know is I was airborne and I went along with it. But I'll tell you, we had some -- I'll tell you what used to bother me more than anything in England. You'd have to get up in the morning and run about two miles. Oh, before breakfast. That used to bother me more than anything, running like that on an empty stomach. But, boy, I'll tell you, you were in good shape when you went in Normandy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you just make that one combat landing in a glider, then?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: That's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The one in Market Square?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were glad you didn't have to do more?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: That's right. That's very true. But the way I see these guys in helicopters now, they might as well be paratroopers. But they just interviewed one General the other day, a new General, and he said, "Our mission is to capture or kill," as far as what they're going in now. And that's what it is. But you don't think about it. You know, I never thought about really -- I was trying to -- of course, again, I wasn't in what you might say the offensive part of it so much as I was keeping -- keeping communication between the groups. That was our main mission. Like one of the -- well, the Sergeant that was in charge of communications and the Sarge of us, I don't know how, he got a battlefield commission. And one of the wiremen -- that's a tough job, laying wire under enemy fire -- he was a commissioned officer, too. So -- but, as I say there --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember getting letters from home from your wife?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah; yeah. But, you see, again, I'd write letters to her, but I couldn't say anything. I mean, everything -- she probably has some of the letters in here. It's scratched out. We were so -- on something all the time. We were very, very -- you didn't have time to think too much about, you know, home and so forth, because there's always activity. Of course, they always had movies. When you're on R and R, there was someplace you could go and they'd have movies there or something. But I never saw any entertainment, like Bob Hope or any of that stuff. I did get into -- I got a leave and I got into Paris, but just one night. And Glenn Miller's band happened to be there. Of course, that was after he was gone. But I'm still a great admirer of his music. Not rock and roll.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Not so much overseas as going over on the boat. That was horrible, oh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the name of the boat you went over on?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I think it was called the Mariposa (ph). I'm not sure. But it got there. But it's a wonder it did get there. But you're so confined and around so many people all the time. I mean, even on the boat going over, you're around people. And then you're in an Army camp over there and you're around people. You know, there's always mobs of people you're around.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Of course, one thing I do remember. I remember climbing down that rope ladder and hitting the beach. I remember that. And, as I told you, I remember the fellows that I'd seen wounded or killed or whatnot. Another time I was in a building somewhere over there -- I don't know where or what country or anything -- and I remember a Jeep drove up. It was frozen winter. And they had a dead guy sticking, you know, in this frozen stuff, just piled in the back of the Jeep. You know, dead bodies they'd picked up. You know, things like that you never forget. Yet, today it bothers me if I see a dog or a cat get hit with a car. I mean, it's so different today. But I'm sorry I can't give you more --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You've given me plenty.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: -- detailed information or more exciting or interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, no, it's very interesting. Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after you came back?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Not really. Not really. I was discharged in Indian Town Gap, Pennsylvania and -- oh, this is funny, too. In Indian Town Gap, Pennsylvania, getting ready to be discharged, we saw these ruptured ducks. And some young -- I don't know, the guys were making noise or something in the barracks. And this young lieutenant comes up the stairs and tells us to shut up. These guys told him to go to hell. He ran down the stairs and never -- of course, all the veterans had been in the war and everything and this little guy is going to come up and tell them, right. A few little things like that you remember. But I was discharged in Indian Town Gap, Pennsylvania. And I -- I remember going, walking out of the camp. I guess I had a barracks bag. I don't remember. And I got on a Greyhound bus, or whatever it was, and met my wife in Pittsburgh. And we spent a couple days in Pittsburgh together before I came home. And, when I came home, it's the first time I saw my oldest son. He was two years old. And, you know, it's so funny, because I was thinking the other day, when we were in Renneker, you know, you have a password when you go in and out of camp.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I can't remember one password. But you had to have it because of the guard at the door.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You remembered it at the time, though?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Oh, I sure did. I surely did. Yeah; yeah. But, you know, I have -- it breaks my heart to see those crosses in Normandy. That gets me. Those are the heroes. Those are the heroes. But, like most of my friends, like Hastings, was wounded. Oh, by the way, a friend of mine was killed, from Penzo (ph), George Sebean (ph). He was with the 327th. And then he was transferred over to the 401st. And he was a warrant officer. And his brother was a priest in Penzo (ph). Sebean (ph) is his name. Very nice. He was killed. When the 401st was coming in to relieve us, he was coming over to see me in a Jeep. The Jeep hit a mine. A great guy. I mean, not us. We were good friends. Friends that I had never known before, but made them in -- most of the friends that I met, believe it or not, and kept in touch with, were those who I met in my very first -- at Cleburne, Camp Cleburne, the first camp I was in. I met Hastings, I met Heflick (ph), who went into the Air Corps. He never went overseas. He comes around to see me. He lives in Indiana. Once in a while he comes around. And Shaffer (ph). And those are the ones that I remember from Camp Cleburne. Now, after Cleburne, there wasn't too many. You know, you didn't get -- I guess it's because everything was brand new to these guys as well. And they're all fine guys. Fine men. Fine men. Bill Grunkenmyer (ph) from Cincinnati. I don't know if he ever went overseas. He was in the radio section. But some of these guys I lost track of. Like my wife knew some of the wives from down there. Like Art Shuck (ph) was a little guy. He was a radio guy. But I don't think he went overseas. A lot of the guys that were at Camp Cleburne, I guess, never went overseas. See, before you got airborne, you could transfer out, you know, like to the Air Corps and stuff like that. When you were in Cleburne, you could make them -- but after you hit Cleburne, we were too hot. I mean, they were really training us solid then. But, as I said, I was happy I could do what I did. And I hope it's sufficient. But I'm a strong believer. You could say anything about military training, but there's nothing wrong with it; nothing wrong with it. You know another thing, too. I never met a gay in the Army. Never.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, they were there, weren't they?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: They must have been.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But you didn't -- yeah.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: I never met -- never, all that I was through, all the training, never. That's why I say, why give them the time? I'll never forget it. Just like the Army says, forget them. As long as they're doing their job, forget them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: But, as I say, I think there's something wrong with them. But, I mean --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But most of them knew to keep their mouth shut?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: Yeah; yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But they were there?

sp.speaker: Alvin H. Karges
sp.p: They were there. They sure were. They surely were. But, as I say, as far as the training the Army gave me, because I never had much trouble discipline-wise anyway -- I mean, my parents were -- I never had any problems in the Army. But, I mean, being with strangers and somebody gives you an order -- I remember really a tough Sergeant. When we got down to Camp Cleburne, he couldn't even pronounce my name. He was some Polish guy. He was a rugged, tough guy. I heard, when we got overseas, when he got into combat he took off. He was really tough over here, though. But, yeah. But I admire the guys in there, I'll tell you. Whether they are in the Army, Navy or what they are, it's the service they're in. They deserve a lot of respect, is all I can say.
